title: Oculogyric crisis in a patient taking metoclopramide
case_prompt:
A 13-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with double vision and involuntary upward and lateral deviation of the eyes that began 30 minutes before presentation. Three days earlier, she had started metoclopramide, 0.5 mg/kg three times daily, for a 2-day history of vomiting. After treatment, her vomiting improved, but she developed the current eye findings.

On examination, she was alert but in severe distress. Neurologic examination showed sustained conjugate upward and lateral deviation of the eyes and neck stiffness limited to the neck muscles; no other dyskinetic movements were observed. She could briefly bring her eyes back to the primary position with extreme effort, but the deviation recurred within seconds. Ophthalmic examination revealed isocoria with intact direct and indirect light reflexes. Ocular motility and visual acuity were not assessable due to the eye deviation. Intraocular pressures, biomicroscopic, and fundoscopic findings were normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. Complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, and electrolytes were within normal values.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered postencephalitic parkinsonism, brainstem encephalitis, Wilson’s disease, and cystic glioma — “although oculogyric crisis usually occurs as a side effect of drugs, it can be seen in patients with postencephalitic parkinsonism, brainstem encephalitis, Wilson’s disease, and cystic glioma, for whom the onset of the crisis is positional.”  
2. Considered versive seizures — “versive seizures with upgaze deviation can simulate oculogyric crises, but they are associated with an alteration of consciousness and electroencephalogram abnormalities.”  
3. Considered paroxysmal tonic upward gaze — “paroxysmal tonic upward gaze ... can be distinguished from oculogyric crisis by the presence of neck flexion and concomitant episodic ataxia.”  
4. Considered eye movement tics — “eye movement tics in children ... are characterized by a stereotyped conjugate deviation of the eyes upward and outward. Oculogyric crisis is more sustained than eye movement tics.”  
5. Recognized drug-induced dystonia given recent metoclopramide use and absence of other neurologic or metabolic abnormalities — “although metoclopramide is used at therapeutic dosages, it may cause acute dystonic reactions at any age,” especially presenting as oculogyric crisis.
